passage: In the one-room school at the edge of a village near Jaipur, Jasleen, five, waved her hand high with her tongue between her teeth. Teacher Rajni was writing on the board and didn't turn. Jasleen's arm began to shake. She almost blurted out, "Miss, Miss!" Then Rajni glanced over and gave a small nod. Jasleen let out her breath and lowered her hand. "Miss, can I go to the toilet?" Rajni nodded, "Go," and Jasleen ran.

qa.q: What did Jasleen ask when Rajni nodded?
qa.a: She asked, "Miss, can I go to the toilet?"

qa.q: What might Jasleen have been feeling while she waited with her hand raised?
qa.a: She was probably restless and anxious, since her arm shook and she nearly blurted out. The nod may have brought her some relief.

qa.q: What could a teacher do to help children wait for a turn?
qa.a: They can give a quick nod or a look to show they have seen the raised hand, even if they can't call on the child yet.

qa.q: How does Rajni see the raised hand while she writes?
qa.a: Rajni might not notice at first because of being busy, but a quick glance and nod lets Jasleen know she is seen.

grounding: A child learns to raise a hand and wait, and a quick nod from the teacher eases her impatience.

passage: In a Warsaw primary school, Marek's hand shot up. "I know! I know!" whispered Marek. Teacher Santiago was helping another child and held up one finger. Marek bounced on his toes, chewing his sleeve, then his hand went up and down. Santiago nodded at him. Marek sat, and when the other child finished, Santiago said, "Marek?" He gave the answer in a rush, cheeks flushed. "Well waited," said Santiago.

qa.q: How did Marek's teacher tell him to wait?
qa.a: Santiago held up one finger.

qa.q: What might Marek have been feeling as he bounced on his toes and chewed his sleeve?
qa.a: He seemed excited and impatient to share his answer, and waiting was hard for him. He might also have been afraid of forgetting it.

qa.q: What could help Marek wait more easily next time?
qa.a: A quick nod from the teacher, as Santiago gave, or a signal that his turn is coming would help.

qa.q: How might the other child helped by Santiago feel while Marek fidgets?
qa.a: That child might feel hurried, so a clear promise to Marek that his turn is next helps both children.

grounding: A child raises a hand to speak and waiting is hard, so the teacher's nod eases frustration.

passage: In the KG classroom, Reena Ma'am was reading about a lost puppy. Pallavi's hand shot up and stayed there. She bounced on her knees, then held her arm up with her other hand. Reena noticed and gave her a quick nod. “One minute, Pallavi, I see you.” Pallavi pressed her knees together and bounced faster. At the end of the page, Reena called on her. “Can I go to the toilet?” Reena smiled. “Of course. Next time you can show me the toilet sign, and go.”

qa.q: What was Reena Ma'am reading about?
qa.a: A lost puppy.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling as she bounced and held her arm up?
qa.a: She was uncomfortable and anxious because she needed the toilet, and it was hard to wait. Her teacher could not tell at first whether it was a question or excitement.

qa.q: What small step did Reena offer so waiting would be easier next time?
qa.a: She suggested a toilet sign, so Pallavi could signal what she needed and go without waiting for her turn to speak.

qa.q: What is it like for Reena to see a hand that stays up for a long time?
qa.a: She has to guess whether it is eagerness, a question or a need, so a quick nod helps the child while she finishes the page.

grounding: A child raises her hand and struggles to wait, the gesture turning out to mean a toilet need, and the teacher's quick nod eases the wait.

passage: I'm Bidisha, a parent helper on reading day. Aadhya sat right in front. Every time the teacher asked a question, she shouted the answer. The teacher reminded her, “Hands up, please.” The next time Aadhya's hand went up so fast she nearly fell over, and she kept saying “Me! Me!” under her breath. The teacher caught her eye and nodded, then called another child first. Aadhya's face crumpled, but she kept her hand up. Next question, the teacher picked her, and her whole face lit up.

qa.q: What did the teacher remind Aadhya to do?
qa.a: Put her hand up.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when her face crumpled?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and disappointed that another child was picked while she was trying so hard to wait. Bidisha could only see her face, so she might also have felt unsure if she would ever get a turn.

qa.q: How did the teacher's nod help Aadhya?
qa.a: It showed Aadhya that her raised hand was seen, which helped her keep waiting instead of blurting out.

qa.q: How might the other children see Aadhya's shouting before she raised her hand?
qa.a: They might feel it was unfair that she answered first each time, which is why hands up gives everyone a turn.

grounding: A parent helper observes a child learning to raise her hand instead of blurting, with the teacher's quick nod easing her frustration.

passage:
Week one: Suraj called out every answer before Farida Miss finished the question. Other children stopped trying.
Week two: Farida Miss taught hands up. Suraj raised his, but waiting was so hard he groaned and slapped the desk. Farida Miss gave him a quick nod each time. “I see you, Suraj. You're next.”
Week three: Suraj raised his hand and waited, lips pressed together, eyes on Farida Miss. When she nodded, he grinned and sat on his hands. When she called him, he said, “Can I say two answers?”

qa.q: What did Suraj do in week one?
qa.a: He called out every answer before Farida Miss finished the question.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling in week two when he groaned and slapped the desk?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and impatient, because he was eager to answer and waiting was hard. The raised hand showed his excitement.

qa.q: Which step helped Suraj most, and why?
qa.a: Farida Miss's quick nod and “You're next” showed him he had been seen, which made waiting easier.

qa.q: How might the other children feel by week three?
qa.a: They would likely feel more willing to answer, since Suraj was no longer calling out first every time.

grounding: Over three weeks, a child learns to raise his hand and wait, with the teacher's nod easing his frustration.

passage:
Five minutes before home time, the rain was so loud on the tin roof that Elizabeth Miss had to shout the spelling words.

Tarun's hand shot up. He wiggled it. He bounced on his seat. He did not call out, though his face was scrunched with the effort.

Elizabeth Miss was bent over another child's slate. Tarun's hand wobbled; he crossed his legs.

At last she looked up, saw him, and gave a quick nod towards the door. Tarun ran for the toilet.

When he came back, she gave him a thumbs up. "Good waiting."

qa.q: How loud was the rain on the tin roof?
qa.a: So loud that Elizabeth Miss had to shout the spelling words.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling while his hand wobbled and he crossed his legs?
qa.a: He was likely uncomfortable and anxious because he urgently needed the toilet, and frustrated by the wait. His scrunched face also shows he was proud to try hard not to call out.

qa.q: What helped end Tarun's frustration quickly?
qa.a: A quick nod towards the door from Elizabeth Miss let him go at once, and her "Good waiting" afterwards praised his effort.

qa.q: What would change if Elizabeth Miss had not looked up for a long time?
qa.a: Tarun might have given up waiting and shouted out, or had an accident, and felt upset about it.

grounding: It shows a child raising his hand and waiting instead of blurting out, and a teacher's quick nod easing the strain.
